transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, Dr. [Name], honestly, I'm only here because my wife insisted, and frankly, it's been a point of contention between us for a while now. You see, for about the past year—maybe a little longer, actually, if I really think back to when it first started—there have been these... patterns. She works as a project manager, and she says the late meetings and the little changes in her work messages are just normal office stuff, you know, just the usual corporate grind. But I've been looking at them, and I mean really looking at them, and they line up too precisely to feel accidental. 

For instance, there was a Tuesday back in October where she said a meeting ran late, but the phrasing in her text message was almost identical to an email she sent me three weeks prior, right down to the specific punctuation. And it’s not just that one time. It’s a consistent thing. It feels like there’s a private signal in them, meant to tell me something she won’t say directly. I’ve tried to explain this to her, how the timing of her late days always coincides with certain shifts in her communication style, but she just brushes it off. She says I'm overthinking it, that I'm reading into things that aren't there. But when you look at the data—and I have, I've kept track of it all because as a teaching assistant, I'm used to analyzing information—it's just too coordinated. It's like she's trying to communicate something to me through these subtle variations, but she refuses to just come out and say it. And so, here I am, because she thinks I need to talk to someone about it, even though I'm just pointing out what's right there in front of us.
When you notice these patterns in her messages, do you see them as truths you're certain about, or do they feel like unwanted thoughts that pop into your head that you try to push away or resist?

Well, no, they certainly aren't unwanted thoughts, and I don't try to push them away at all. Why would I? I mean, I'm just observing what's actually happening. It's not like these are random ideas popping into my head out of nowhere. I'm looking at the evidence. I know my wife says the late meetings and little changes in her work messages are just normal office stuff, you know, she always says, "Oh, it's just the corporate grind, honey, you're overthinking it." But I'm not overthinking it, I'm just reading what's there. 

For the past year, these things have lined up too precisely to feel accidental. Like, if it happens once, sure, maybe it's a coincidence. But when the phrasing in a text about a late meeting on a Tuesday matches an email from three weeks prior, down to the exact placement of a semicolon? That's not a coincidence. That's a pattern. It's like there's a private signal in them, meant to tell me something she won't say directly. And I don't resist seeing it because it's the truth. I'm just trying to understand what the signal actually means, since she refuses to just sit down and explain it to me plainly. If she would just be direct, I wouldn't have to spend so much time analyzing the texts, but since she won't, I have to pay attention to these variations. So no, I don't push the thoughts away, because they are real, tangible things I'm observing in her communication.
Aside from these patterns you notice in her messages, have you ever heard voices, sounds, or seen things that other people around you don't seem to hear or see?

No, no, nothing like that. I mean, I'm not crazy, Doctor. I don't hear voices whispering in my ear or see things floating in the corner of the room. It's nothing... hallucinatory, if that's what you're asking. I know sometimes people who pay close attention to things get lumped into that category, but that's not me at all. My senses are perfectly fine. Better than fine, really, considering how much I pick up on. 

Like I said, what I'm dealing with is entirely based on real, physical evidence. Things you could look at yourself if I showed you my phone or pulled up the emails on my laptop. It's the texts, the punctuation, the timestamps—those are all completely real. Anyone with eyes could see them. Now, whether anyone else would take the time to actually sit down, cross-reference the dates, and notice the deliberate repetition of certain phrases... well, that's a different story. Most people are too busy or too distracted to notice the subtleties of language, especially in something as mundane as a text saying, "Running late, start dinner without me." But I notice. Because as a teaching assistant, grading papers and reading through student essays all day, my brain is literally trained to catch inconsistencies, repeated structures, and hidden meanings. So no, I don't hear voices. I just read what's right in front of me, even if my wife won't admit she's the one putting it there.

Aside from your wife, have you generally had a longstanding pattern—going back to your teens or early adulthood—of feeling that other people, like friends, coworkers, or family, are being deceptive or hiding things from you?

No, not at all. I mean, if we're talking about my teens or my twenties, or really any time before this past year, I was always pretty trusting. Maybe too trusting, honestly, but no, I never had any issues with friends or family. I mean, my parents, my brother, my coworkers at the university—I've never felt like they were hiding anything or being deceptive. We've always had very straightforward relationships. I've been at the university for over a decade now, working with different professors, and it's always been very clear-cut. They give me the syllabus, I grade the papers, we discuss the rubrics. There's no hidden agenda there. And with my friends, we just watch the game or grab a beer. It's very surface-level, very normal. 

This whole situation... it's strictly with my wife. And it's not like I woke up one day and just decided to start suspecting her of things. It really all traces back to when she got promoted to project manager last year. Before that, her texts were just normal texts. "Can you pick up milk?" or "I'll be home at six." But once she started managing that new team, the language shifted. It became more formal, more structured, and that's when the repetition started. That's when I noticed the semicolon usage changing, and the specific phrasing about "circling back" or "touching base later" that always seemed to coincide with her late nights. It's very isolated to her and to this specific timeframe. I don't walk around thinking the barista at the coffee shop is sending me coded messages in my latte art, or that my brother is lying to me about his golf score to cover up some secret life. It's just her, and it's just these messages, because the data is right there. If anyone else was doing it, I'd notice, but they aren't. It's just her.
